Menstrual cycles and the burden of asking without explaining

Perhaps the most striking gap is the absence of any normalized conversation about menstrual cycles and bathroom access. Women officers need to request time away from their posts or duties for personal hygiene during their cycles, but the workplace culture offers no framework for this discussion. When a woman must ask a supervisor for time without being able to explain why—either because she's uncomfortable speaking about her cycle or because the workplace has made clear such topics are unwelcome—she is placed in an impossible position.

This forced silence creates practical and emotional consequences. A woman cannot simply take bathroom time when she needs it the way a male officer can. The details matter: menstrual products may need changing during a shift, or a woman may need to manage leakage or discomfort without announcing the reason to her supervisor. The burden of managing this privately, without support or acknowledgment, adds an invisible layer of stress to an already demanding job. A detailed discussion of how women navigate these specific workplace barriers is explored in depth in this podcast episode .

The foundation of decisive leadership rests on five concrete practices you must undertake long before any emergency surfaces. Know where expertise lives in your organization and identify it by name, not by title.

Understanding your terrain and building intelligence

Understand the environment in which you operate. Ask questions before the crisis arrives—not defensively, but to genuinely comprehend the landscape, the constraints, and the opportunities. Learn from every situation you've already handled , extracting lessons about consequences, timing, and what works in your specific context.

The real preparation happens months in advance—when you are taking on tasks others are not, when your boss is nudging you toward advancement, and when your team is rooting for your success. Self-doubt is remarkably common among capable professionals. Your boss's encouragement is the clearest signal

When your supervisor is actively encouraging you to apply for a promotion, they see something you may not see in yourself. They work with you daily and understand your capabilities. That encouragement is not casual—it is evidence. A boss who invests time in pushing you forward has already assessed your readiness; they are not wasting effort on someone unprepared.

The Three-Step Formula That Works

The traditional approach of formally asking someone to be your mentor can feel uncomfortable for both parties. This cycle works because it demonstrates two qualities mentors look for in mentees. First, you show you're willing to listen and act —not just collect advice passively. Second, you close the loop by reporting results, which gives the mentor concrete proof that their guidance had real impact.
Why Ambitious People Attract Mentors

The hidden advantage of this approach is that people are naturally drawn to helping those who take action . When someone implements your suggestion and comes back with a success story, you feel invested in their growth. You've already seen them execute once, which removes doubt about whether they're serious.

f: Read the full job announcement from top to bottom — every qualification, every preferred experience, every Knowledge, Skill, and Ability (KSA) listed. Then map your own background directly onto those requirements, and pinpoint what you bring that no other candidate does. The announcement is not just a checklist: it tells you exactly what problem the organization is trying to solve, and your job is to show you are the solution.
The job announcement already contains the answer — most candidates just don't read it carefully enough

A job announcement is a precise brief from the hiring panel. It names the qualifications they require, the experience they prefer, and the competencies they expect. Yet most candidates skim it once and move on to polishing their résumé.

Marie Sonneman, host of Ordinary To Badass , is direct about this: the announcement tells you exactly what the panel needs. Your entire preparation should be organized around those signals — not around what you happen to find easy to talk about.

Reading for the problem the role is meant to solve is especially important. Every open position exists because something needs fixing, improving, or scaling. Candidates who address that underlying need — not just the listed bullet points — stand out immediately.
From matching requirements to owning your differentiator

f071d215cf.q: How can workplace categories and reputation limit career advancement opportunities?
f071d215cf.a: Once people have enough evidence to put you in a category, their brains get lazy. If you are seen as the technical expert but want to become a leader, they…
f071d215cf.e: 454: 8 Leadership Lessons from Women Who Changed the Room | Part 1
f: Once people categorize you professionally, your brain gets lazy and theirs do too —they stop seeing potential beyond what they already know. If you want to break free from that category, you cannot wait passively; you must actively provide evidence of the new capabilities you want to be known for, whether that's leadership, decision-making, handling conflict, or developing others.

The trap is real: you become known for one thing—the technical expert, the reliable operator, the specialist—and that label hardens into a ceiling. People's minds organize you into a box, and that cognitive shortcut becomes their default . They see you through that filter because it's efficient for their brains. Breaking out requires more than competence; it demands visibility and proof.

Waiting for someone to "discover" a hidden side of you does not work. You must take concrete action—volunteer for projects outside your category, offer ideas in meetings, step into leadership roles, and let people see you making decisions and handling real conflict. Each action is a data point that challenges the old story they told themselves about who you are.

As explored in this episode of Ordinary To Badass , this lesson emerges from studying how women like Oprah Winfrey and Ruth Bader Ginsburg navigated rigid perceptions and shifted how others saw them through deliberate action and ownership.
The category trap and how brains lock you in

The moment you accumulate enough evidence in one domain, people's brains move into a kind of holding pattern. Cognitive ease takes over —they have a filed-away mental image of you, and they stop updating it. This is not malice; it is how human brains work when information is already organized.

cc1e5109b2.q: Why is building career leverage more powerful than making yourself valuable to a single organization?
cc1e5109b2.a: If you build all your value inside one system, one boss controls your opportunities, one organization controls your title, and one person controls whether…
cc1e5109b2.e: 454: 8 Leadership Lessons from Women Who Changed the Room | Part 1
f: If you build all your value inside one system, one boss controls your opportunities, one organization controls your title, and one person controls whether you're ready. Career leverage—your knowledge, relationships, reputation, experience, ability to solve problems, communication skills, judgment, and body of work—belongs to you alone , not to any employer.
What Actually Stays with You

The fundamental question is this: if your title disappeared tomorrow, what would still belong to you? Organizations change. Bosses move on. Corporate structures reorganize. But the skills, relationships, and reputation you've built exist independently of any single institution.

Career leverage is built on assets you own outright —not credentials issued by someone else, not authority granted by a hierarchy. When you focus exclusively on being valuable to one organization, you're betting everything on that single relationship continuing. The moment it ends—through layoff, restructuring, or your own departure—you lose access to the titles, resources, and opportunities that organization controlled.

As Marie Sonneman explores in this episode , women who changed their fields—like Oprah Winfrey—understood this principle early. They didn't stop at being the best performer within someone else's system; they built ownership of their own career assets.
The Danger of Organizational Dependence

a7f67ee446.q: How did Oprah Winfrey build career leverage beyond simply being talented and valuable?
a7f67ee446.a: Oprah moved from being the talent working inside somebody else's machine to becoming an owner. She built Harpo Productions and gained ownership and…
a7f67ee446.e: 454: 8 Leadership Lessons from Women Who Changed the Room | Part 1
f: Oprah moved from being the talent working inside somebody else's machine to becoming an owner through Harpo Productions . By gaining production control over her show, she transformed her relationship with her employer and built leverage that gave her options beyond dependence on one boss or organization.

The shift from employee to owner fundamentally changed how Oprah negotiated her power. When Marie Sonneman explores this strategy in the episode , she emphasizes that Oprah's move was deliberate: she didn't wait to be handed control—she built the infrastructure to gain it. Talent alone gets you a paycheck. Ownership gets you leverage.
Control over the product itself

The critical move was gaining control over production , not just performance. Oprah didn't just deliver her talent to a network; she controlled what was being made, how it was made, and who profited from it. This distinction matters because it means she wasn't replaceable in the same way a talent confined to performance would be.

By owning Harpo Productions, Oprah changed the entire dynamic of her career negotiations. She had options. She could take the show elsewhere, control its quality, and determine its future. A network couldn't simply swap her out without losing the property itself. This is how the podcast illustrates career leverage in practice —not through scarcity of talent, but through control of an asset.

This strategy reveals why many talented people never build lasting power: they remain replaceable. Oprah built a moat around her influence by being not just irreplaceable talent, but the owner of the enterprise that delivered the talent. When the Oprah Winfrey Show went national in 1986, she had already begun structuring ownership that would define her decades of influence to come.

ee9a412b46.q: How did Ruth Bader Ginsburg use strategic audience understanding to influence an all-male Supreme Court on gender discrimination cases?
ee9a412b46.a: Ginsburg brought cases involving men harmed by gender bias laws, such as Stephen Weisensfeld, whose wife died during childbirth. She helped the all-male…
ee9a412b46.e: 454: 8 Leadership Lessons from Women Who Changed the Room | Part 1
f: Ginsburg didn't argue gender discrimination only from women's perspectives—she brought cases involving men harmed by discriminatory laws, letting an all-male bench experience bias from a direction they could personally understand . The strategy worked: the Supreme Court unanimously ruled in favor of Stephen Weisensfeld, whose wife died during childbirth, in a landmark case that advanced gender equality through the justices' own lived recognition of injustice.

Ginsburg's approach reveals a fundamental principle of persuasion: being right and being influential are not the same thing. An advocate can hold the strongest legal argument imaginable and still fail to move a decision-maker who cannot see themselves in the problem. The Weisensfeld case showed that sometimes the most powerful way to change a room is to reframe the issue so decision-makers see their own interests at stake .

When Ginsburg argued before the Supreme Court in the 1970s, she faced a structural barrier: nine male justices with no lived experience of gender discrimination as women experience it. Rather than accept this as an insurmountable obstacle, as described in this episode on leadership strategy , she strategically selected cases where men were the direct victims of gender-based laws. The case of Weisensfeld, a man denied Social Security survivors' benefits because those benefits were designed to favor widows over widowers, gave the justices a concrete human story—a grieving father fighting for his right to care for his child without bureaucratic punishment.

This wasn't about watering down the feminist argument or abandoning women's equality. Instead, Ginsburg recognized that unanimous support from an all-male court was worth more than a divided ruling with ideological allies . By choosing cases where men were harmed, she demonstrated that gender discrimination laws hurt the entire system of justice, not just one group. The unanimity of the Weisensfeld ruling sent a powerful message: this was not a partisan issue, but a matter of constitutional principle.

The deeper lesson, explored more broadly in this discussion of women who changed entire rooms , is that strategic audience understanding requires ego to take a back seat. Ginsburg could have insisted on making every case about women's suffering and women's rights—a morally sound position. Instead, she chose the harder path: understanding what language, what evidence, what human story would actually move her specific audience. That flexibility didn't compromise her goal; it accelerated it.
Meeting decision-makers where they can hear you
